story.hook: One tiny email exposed my manager's fake rule.
story.script: For three weeks, my manager had everyone staying late because he kept saying head office had made two hours of overtime mandatory. Nobody had seen the policy, but every evening at six he would stand near the door and remind us that leaving on time would be noted during performance reviews. Most people complained quietly and stayed. I did too at first. Then one Thursday, he sent another message saying the rule was non-negotiable, so I replied politely and asked for the policy number because I wanted to make sure I recorded the overtime correctly. He told me not to overcomplicate things and said the instruction came directly from head office. That was when I forwarded the message to payroll and asked which code I should use on my timesheet. Payroll replied twenty minutes later. There was no mandatory overtime policy, there was no special code, and any approved overtime had to be requested in advance and paid. They copied HR into the reply. Suddenly my manager stopped answering the chat. The next morning, HR asked our team for copies of every message about the supposed rule. By lunch, the pinned announcement about mandatory overtime had disappeared, and a new message appeared saying everyone should follow their normal contracted hours unless overtime was formally approved. My manager tried to call it a misunderstanding, but the email trail was very clear. He had invented the rule because our project was behind schedule and he did not want to explain the delay upward. The best part was that payroll also asked everyone to submit the extra hours we had already worked so they could review payment. I had only asked for a policy number. Instead, one ordinary email ended the fake rule, got HR involved, and turned all those unpaid late nights into a problem my manager had to explain himself.

youtube.description: A manager invents an unpaid overtime rule, until one simple email reaches payroll. An original Wacky Dramas story.
